pos: n. (proper name; owner or teacher of a lecture hall at Ephesus)
etymology: Greek Tyrannos, sovereign, ruler, the word from which English takes tyrant; in the Greek world it first meant simply an absolute ruler.
biblical_def: Tyrannus is the man in whose lecture hall the gospel was taught daily at Ephesus. Paul had spoken in the synagogue “for the space of three months, disputing and persuading the things concerning the kingdom of God” (Acts 19:8), but when some hardened themselves and spoke evil of the Way before the crowd, he withdrew. “He departed from them, and separated the disciples, disputing daily in the school of one Tyrannus” (Acts 19:9). Luke names the room and nothing more; whether Tyrannus was a teacher who rented his hall or the owner of the building, the Spirit did not record. What He did record is the fruit: “this continued by the space of two years; so that all they which dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks” (Acts 19:10). A borrowed classroom in a pagan city became the base from which a whole province heard the gospel. The churches of Asia addressed in Revelation 2–3 trace their roots to those two years of daily, patient teaching in the school of Tyrannus.

etymology: Latin Tiberius, a Roman praenomen usually connected with the river Tiber.
biblical_def: Tiberius Caesar is the emperor by whose reign Luke dates the beginning of John the Baptist's ministry: “Now in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judaea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee” (Luke 3:1). Luke is a historian, and he anchors the gospel in the calendar of the world. Against the names of the mighty, emperor, governor, tetrarchs and high priests, the decisive event of the year happens in a desert: “the word of God came unto John the son of Zacharias in the wilderness” (Luke 3:2). Tiberius was the Caesar of the whole public ministry of Christ; his image was on the coin when Jesus said, “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Matthew 22:21), and it was to his friendship that Pilate feared to be found disloyal at the trial. The lake city of Tiberias in Galilee was named for him. Scripture records him not to honor him but to fix the gospel in real time: the Son of God came under a named emperor, in a datable year.

pos: n. (proper name; a rebel leader cited by Gamaliel)
etymology: Greek Theudas, probably a short form of a name such as Theodorus, gift of God.
biblical_def: Theudas is the would-be deliverer whom Gamaliel named before the council when the apostles were on trial. “For before these days rose up Theudas, boasting himself to be somebody; to whom a number of men, about four hundred, joined themselves: who was slain; and all, as many as obeyed him, were scattered, and brought to nought” (Acts 5:36). Gamaliel added Judas of Galilee, who “also perished” (Acts 5:37), and drew his counsel: “if this counsel or this work be of men, it will come to nought” (Acts 5:38). Theudas is the type of the false messiah: self-exalting, followed for a season, and gone. His movement had a leader and four hundred men; it lacked only God. The apostles had a crucified and risen Lord, and their work could not be overthrown. Gamaliel's counsel was prudent but incomplete; the question is never only whether a movement survives, but whether its Christ is the true one.

pos: n. (proper name; wife of Ananias in the Jerusalem church)
etymology: Aramaic shappira, beautiful; the Greek form is close to sappheiros, sapphire.
biblical_def: Sapphira is the wife of Ananias, who with him lied to the Holy Ghost. “But a certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira his wife, sold a possession” (Acts 5:1), kept back part of the price, and laid the rest at the apostles' feet as though it were the whole. Peter exposed the sin as Satanic: “why hath Satan filled thine heart to lie to the Holy Ghost” (Acts 5:3). Ananias fell dead. About three hours later Sapphira came in, not knowing, and confirmed the same lie. Peter answered, “How is it that ye have agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord? behold, the feet of them which have buried thy husband are at the door, and shall carry thee out” (Acts 5:9). Her name means beautiful, and her sin was outward beauty over inward deceit: a show of generosity concealing love of money and love of praise. The sin was not keeping the money, which was theirs, but lying to God. “And great fear came upon all the church” (Acts 5:11). She is the first named woman in Acts after the women at prayer, and a solemn warning that the Spirit dwelling in the church is holy.

pos: n. and adj. (a native of Phoenicia under Syria)
etymology: Greek Syrophoinikissa, a woman of Syrophoenicia, the Phoenician coast of Tyre and Sidon reckoned to the province of Syria.
biblical_def: Syrophenician describes the Gentile mother whose faith Christ honored in the borders of Tyre and Sidon. “The woman was a Greek, a Syrophenician by nation; and she besought him that he would cast forth the devil out of her daughter” (Mark 7:26). Mark gives both her culture, Greek, and her race, Syrophenician, so that no reader misses that she stood outside Israel. Jesus answered, “Let the children first be filled: for it is not meet to take the children's bread, and to cast it unto the dogs” (Mark 7:27). She did not argue her worthiness; she accepted the word and pleaded from it: “Yes, Lord: yet the dogs under the table eat of the children's crumbs” (Mark 7:28). That is the humility of faith, which agrees with God's verdict and then casts itself on His mercy. “For this saying go thy way; the devil is gone out of thy daughter” (Mark 7:29). Matthew calls her a woman of Canaan. Her crumbs became a foretaste of the Gentile feast the gospel would spread to the nations.

pos: n. pl. (people of Parthia, east of Mesopotamia)
etymology: Greek Parthoi, the people of Parthia, the Iranian kingdom beyond the Euphrates that rivalled Rome.
biblical_def: Parthians head the list of nations present at Pentecost. “Parthians, and Medes, and Elamites, and the dwellers in Mesopotamia, and in Judaea, and Cappadocia, in Pontus, and Asia” (Acts 2:9). There were dwelling at Jerusalem “Jews, devout men, out of every nation under heaven” (Acts 2:5), and the Parthians among them were Jews of the eastern dispersion, descendants of the exiles carried to Assyria and Babylon who had never returned. Parthia was Rome's great rival in the east, a kingdom the legions could not conquer. The gospel reached it on its first day. Each heard the apostles in his own tongue, “the wonderful works of God” (Acts 2:11). Babel scattered the nations by confusing their speech; Pentecost gathered them by the Spirit, and the list begins from the far east. The Lord who said His disciples would be witnesses to the uttermost part of the earth began with men from beyond the reach of Caesar.

pos: n. (proper name; a province on the south coast of Asia Minor)
etymology: Greek Lykia, the mountainous coastal land between Caria and Pamphylia.
biblical_def: Lycia is the coastal province where Paul changed ships on his voyage as a prisoner to Rome. “And when we had sailed over the sea of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra, a city of Lycia” (Acts 27:5). The winds had been against them from the start: “we sailed under Cyprus, because the winds were contrary” (Acts 27:4). At Myra the centurion “found a ship of Alexandria sailing into Italy; and he put us therein” (Acts 27:6), one of the grain ships that fed Rome. That ship carried Paul into the storm and the wreck on Melita. Patara, where Paul had earlier changed ships on his way to Jerusalem (Acts 21:1), also lay in Lycia. The province appears in Scripture only as a waypoint, yet God's providence ran through every harbor: the ship found at Myra was the ship on which He would show His power to save every soul aboard, and by which He brought His servant to bear witness in Rome.

pos: n. (proper name; the Roman messenger god, Greek Hermes)
etymology: Latin Mercurius, the Roman god of messages and commerce, rendering the Greek Hermes of the original.
biblical_def: Mercurius is the name the crowd at Lystra gave to Paul. When Paul healed a man crippled from birth, the people lifted up their voices “saying in the speech of Lycaonia, The gods are come down to us in the likeness of men” (Acts 14:11). “And they called Barnabas, Jupiter; and Paul, Mercurius, because he was the chief speaker” (Acts 14:12). In their mythology the messenger god spoke for the chief god, and Paul did the preaching. The priest of Jupiter brought oxen and garlands to sacrifice. The apostles were horrified: “they rent their clothes, and ran in among the people” (Acts 14:14), crying, “We also are men of like passions with you, and preach unto you that ye should turn from these vanities unto the living God” (Acts 14:15). The scene exposes idolatry at its root: fallen man, seeing the power of God, worships the creature instead. Paul would not receive the glory that belongs to God alone.

pos: n. (proper name; son of Zerubbabel in Luke's genealogy)
biblical_def: Rhesa is a son of Zerubbabel named in the genealogy of Christ in Luke: “Which was the son of Joanna, which was the son of Rhesa, which was the son of Zorobabel, which was the son of Salathiel, which was the son of Neri” (Luke 3:27). Luke traces the line backward from “Jesus himself” (Luke 3:23) through David to Adam. Rhesa stands one generation below Zerubbabel, the governor whom God called His signet: “will I take thee, O Zerubbabel, my servant, the son of Shealtiel, saith the LORD, and will make thee as a signet” (Haggai 2:23). Nothing else is recorded of Rhesa. Yet the line passed through him, and every name in it witnesses that the Son was “made of the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:3). The genealogies are not filler; they are God's proof that His promise to David kept its course through exile and return to the manger.

pos: n. (proper name; father of Anna the prophetess)
biblical_def: Phanuel is the father of Anna, the aged widow who met the infant Christ in the temple. “And there was one Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Aser” (Luke 2:36). His name is the Hebrew Penuel, face of God, the place where Jacob said he had seen God face to face. Luke records him for his daughter's sake and for his tribe: Asher was one of the northern tribes scattered by Assyria, yet the family had kept its genealogy, and an Asherite woman was among the first to see the salvation of Israel. Anna “departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day” (Luke 2:37), and when she saw the child she “spake of him to all them that looked for redemption in Jerusalem” (Luke 2:38). The father whose name meant the face of God had a daughter who lived to see God's face in the flesh.

corruption_summary: The northern tribes are called lost; Phanuel's family of Asher kept its line and saw the redemption of Israel.
corruption_paragraphs: Popular speculation about the ten lost tribes ignores the testimony of Scripture that members of the northern tribes remained within Israel. Anna, daughter of Phanuel of Asher, is one such witness.
This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God keeps a remnant from every tribe. “Of the tribe of Aser were sealed twelve thousand” (Revelation 7:6).
roots_summary: Greek Phanouel, Hebrew Penuel, face of God; Asherite father of Anna.
roots_lines: Hebrew Penu'el, face of God.
Father of Anna the prophetess (Luke 2:36).
Of the tribe of Aser.
His daughter served in the temple night and day.
She spoke of Christ to all who looked for redemption.
